title: Reactivity Series and Extraction of Metals

blocks.text: Gold nuggets are dug from the ground already shining, iron has to be smelted at 1500 degrees Celsius, and aluminium was a precious metal until someone invented a way to electrolyse it. One list explains all three, and it is the reactivity series.

blocks.title: The activity series
blocks.text: The activity or reactivity series arranges metals in order of the ease with which they lose electrons to form positive ions. The most reactive metals are at the top and the least reactive at the bottom. Hydrogen is included as a reference point even though it is not a metal.

rows: Very slow cold, fast with steam
blocks.caption: The activity series with reactions and extraction methods

blocks.markdown:
## Displacement

A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt, because the more reactive metal has the stronger tendency to give up electrons.

Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> ZnSO4(aq) + Cu(s)

The blue colour of the copper(II) sulphate fades and a brown deposit of copper appears on the zinc. Reverse the pair and nothing happens: copper cannot displace zinc, because copper is lower in the series.

**Rule: a metal displaces any metal below it in the series, and no metal above it.**

blocks.title: Predicting a displacement reaction
blocks.prompt: Iron filings are added to (i) copper(II) sulphate solution and (ii) magnesium sulphate solution. Predict what happens in each case and write an equation where a reaction occurs.

steps.text: Locate the metals in the series. The order from most to least reactive here is magnesium, then iron, then copper.
For (i), iron is above copper, so iron can displace copper from its salt. A reaction occurs.
Observation for (i): the blue solution fades to pale green as iron(II) sulphate forms, and a brown-pink deposit of copper appears on the filings.
Equation for (i): Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s).
For (ii), iron is below magnesium, so iron cannot displace magnesium. There is no reaction and no visible change.
In redox terms, in (i) iron is oxidised from 0 to +2 while copper is reduced from +2 to 0. Every displacement reaction is a redox reaction.

blocks.answer: Iron displaces copper, giving FeSO4 and a brown copper deposit; there is no reaction with magnesium sulphate

blocks.markdown:
## Matching the extraction method to the position

A metal in its ore is present as a positive ion, so extraction always means **reduction**. How hard that is depends on how tightly the metal holds its ions together with the anion.

- **Very reactive metals** (potassium to aluminium) form very stable compounds that carbon cannot reduce, so **electrolysis of the molten compound** is used. Aluminium comes from purified bauxite dissolved in molten cryolite, which lowers the working temperature from over 2000 to about 950 degrees Celsius.
- **Moderately reactive metals** (zinc, iron, lead) can be reduced by **carbon or carbon monoxide** in a furnace. In the blast furnace: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2.
- **Unreactive metals** (copper, silver, gold) are found native or need only **roasting** the ore in air.

The pattern is simple: the higher the metal in the series, the more energy its extraction requires.

blocks.title: Rusting and its prevention
blocks.text: Rusting is the oxidation of iron in the presence of both oxygen and water to form hydrated iron(III) oxide. Remove either one and rusting stops. Prevention methods include painting, greasing, galvanising with zinc and sacrificial protection using blocks of a more reactive metal such as zinc or magnesium, which corrode instead of the iron.

blocks.title: Justify with the series
blocks.text: When a question asks whether a reaction will occur, name both metals and their relative positions. 'Zinc is above copper in the activity series, so zinc displaces copper' earns the mark; 'yes, a reaction occurs' does not.

points: The activity series ranks metals by how readily they lose electrons to form positive ions.
A metal displaces any metal below it in the series from a solution of that metal's salt.
Only metals above hydrogen liberate hydrogen from dilute acids.
Metals above zinc are extracted by electrolysis of their molten compounds.
Zinc, iron and lead are extracted by reduction with carbon or carbon monoxide.
Rusting requires both oxygen and water, and is prevented by barriers or by sacrificial protection.
